newsitem.title: USA: Russian space probe likely to hit Australia - U.S..
newsitem.headline: Russian space probe likely to hit Australia - U.S..

text.p: A disabled Russian space probe is expected to fall to earth in east-central Australia at about 8:12 p.m. EST on Sunday (0112 GMT Monday), but damage is likely to be minimal, a senior White House official said.

Robert Bell, a U.S. National Security Council official, told reporters with President Bill Clinton on a trip to Asia that the expected impact zone of the Mars probe, which has batteries containing radioactive plutonium, was "in the central to eastern part of Australia, which would be somewhere north of Canberra."

Bell said the track of the stricken space vehicle was being monitored and updated constantly, and if the fall to earth occurred just one minute later than expected, the debris would plunge into the Pacific Ocean "somewhere east of Australia.

The probe weighed about seven tons at launch, including fuel, and most of it was expected to burn up on re-entering earth's atmosphere, Bell said in a telephone conference call from Washington. But he said two penetrating vehicles of 400 to 500 pounds each were expected to survive re-entry and crash to earth in a relatively uninhabited region of Australia.
Bell said the re-entry vehicles each carried two tiny plutonium batteries about the size of 35mm film cannisters containing a total of 200 grams of the radioactive material.

"The Russian space agency has informed NASA that these batteries are designed to withstand great heat and great stress on impact," Bell said. He said Russian assessments that there was little danger of radioactive contamination of the environment was "very reassuring."
Clinton, who conferred by telephone with Australian Prime Minister John Howard on Sunday morning about the situation, is scheduled to begin a five-day visit to Australia on Monday.

Asked if the Russian space mishap would affect the president's trip, Bell replied: "We don't expect it will affect the president's trip at all. We hope that if it (the probe) does impact Australia, there will be very limited damage."

Bell said Clinton had offered Howard "assets we have in the Department of Energy" to deal with such mishaps, and that he himself had spoken by telephone to other Australian officials about the situation.

The Russian probe lifted off from Kazakhstan's Baikonur space centre on Saturday at 11.48 p.m. Moscow time (3:48 p.m. EST). It had been due to reach Mars on Sept. 12 next year. The failed mission was the second of three planned trips from Earth to Mars in just over a month.
The United States launched a robot voyage to Mars two weeks ago and a second mission will blast off on Dec. 2.
All were tasked to check for signs of water on the far-away planet -- a key clue to whether there was once life on Mars.
Bell said a misfiring of a fourth stage of the probe's booster rocket had doomed the Russian Mars probe.
The U.S. Space Command "is now estimating that the spacecraft will reenter the earth's atmosphere just after 8 PM EST (0010 GMT) tonight," the U.S. official said.
Bell said there were "a couple of scenarios that could be a worst case," but stressed all were "extremely unlikely."
One was that the plutonium canisters would break up on re- entry. If this happened at high altitude, Bell said a small radioactive cloud that would result would dissipate harmlessly.

"If some cloud of dispersal were formed at a lower altitude and inhaled by humans, it could be lethal," Bell said. He said there could also be a localised danger if the canisters broke up upon impact.

"But again, we're talking about a very modest amount of plutonium ... a total of about 200 grams. And it's hard for me to imagine that even if it's diffused into some sort of small cloud that it would be a very large area covered by this," said Bell, who is a special assistant to the president and a senior director of the NSC for defence policy.

The Russian space mishap was believed to be the third incident of its kind in recent years. A U.S. space vehicle called Skylab and plunged to earth over Western Australia in 1979 without causing damage and a Russian satellite fell to earth in an unhabited region of Canada, experts said.
